name: Mongolian
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Harnud, Huhe. 2004. Stress on Mongolian trisyllabic words. In: Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2004 (Nara, Japan, 23-26 March 2004), pp. 61-64. ISCA. DOI 10.21437/SpeechProsody.2004-14. Corroborating (same speakers): Harnud, Huhe. 2003. Stress on Mongolian disyllabic words. Proc. 15th ICPhS, Barcelona, pp. 2433-2436.
catalog_locator: Proceedings pp. 61-64 (ISCA archive record: pages 61-64; the PDF itself carries no page numbers). Sec. 3.2 'Results' and sec. 4 'Conclusions' points 4(a), 5 and 6 are on p. 2 = p. 62; speakers sec. 2.1 'Method', p. 1 = p. 61; Fig. 4 perception ratios, p. 4 = p. 64; F0 'L-L-H' and intensity 'W-W-S' patterns for S-S-L in secs. 2.2.2-2.2.3, pp. 1-2. Disyllable rule: Harnud 2003 sec. 5 'Conclusions' (4) and sec. 4.3 are on p. 3 = p. 2435 (the pages carry printed numbers 2433-2436; p. 2434 carries only the sec. 3.3 perception result)
catalog_quote: the following conclusion can be reached on the basis of the total ratio of the three groups and taking into account the acoustic parameters: the placement of the stress depends on the quantity pattern (word type): if a trisyllabic word belongs to the S-S-S, S-S-L, S-L-S or S-L-L type, the second syllable is stressed, but if it belongs to the L-L-L, L-L-S, L-S-L or L-S-S type, the first syllable has been perceived stressed. ... 4) The evaluations of the three groups show that: (a) the placements of stress depend on the vowel quantity patterns in that if a trisyllabic word belongs to the S-S-S, S-S-L, S-L-S or S-L-L type, i.e., if it has a short vowel in the first syllable, the second syllable will be stressed, and if a trisyllabic word belongs to the L-L-L, L-L-S, L-S-L or L-S-S type, i.e., if it has a long vowel in the first syllable, the first syllable will be stressed. ... 5) Mongolian belongs to the Altaic language family is a quantity language with a phonological distinction in vowels and therefore duration cannot be used freely for word stress correlate (as opposite to Russian). F0 and intensity can make the second syllable more prominent than the first. Intensity seems to be the most regular correlate of word stress. 6) Mongolian word stress is free (moveable), but it has no distinctive function. It is not free in the sense that a speaker could deliberately place it on any syllable randomly, but is conventionally fixed on certain syllables.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and its position is predictable from vowel quantity: a word whose first syllable has a long vowel is stressed on the first syllable; a word whose first syllable has a short vowel is stressed on the second syllable (for disyllables Harnud 2003 gives the same rule: S-S and S-L -> second syllable, L-L and L-S -> first syllable; Harnud et al. 2000: 'first stress in long-long, long-short types.. second stress in short-short, short-long types'). Intensity and F0 are the cues that make the second syllable prominent; duration cannot serve freely as a stress cue because vowel length is phonemic. By contrast the older Ordos descriptions (Mostaert 1926 p. 853; Soulié 1903 p. 18) and the Inner Mongolian grammatical tradition (Cinggeltei 1991, as cited by Gao 2020 and Harnud 2000) put a dynamic accent regularly on the first syllable, with a shift to a long vowel in the second syllable when the first is short.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Harnud: none discussed. Mostaert 1927 p. 175 mentions an 'accent secondaire' on the final syllable of certain forms (e.g. before a pause, emphatic forms); Mostaert 1926 p. 853: in emphatic speech the final syllable, whose vowel can be lengthened at will, may carry a dynamic accent combined with a tonic (pitch) accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Harnud 2004: for the L-L-S type the three speakers gave three different intensity patterns; F0 and intensity make the second syllable prominent in short-initial words; perception groups (Mongolian linguists vs. naive vs. Han Chinese students) differ in ratios. Mostaert 1926 p. 853 (Ordos): 'L'accent dynamique n'est pas marqué, puisqu'il vient se placer régulièrement sur la première syllabe. Cependant.. dans les mots à première syllabe brève et dont la seconde syllabe est portée par une voyelle longue, il peut arriver que l'accent dynamique vienne se placer sur celle-ci'; clitic-like words in the phrase may lose their main accent; Ordos accent weaker than in Khalkha, Tumet, Chakhar and Jehol Mongol. Soulié 1903 p. 18 (Ordos): accent on the first syllable of di-/trisyllables except when the 2nd/3rd syllables are diphthongs (long vowels). Gao 2020 (Khorchin): F0 and intensity peak on the last syllable; initial syllable prominent only in duration/articulation; probably word-level pitch accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, isolated words in a fixed carrier sentence ('This is a horse') in focus position; 188 trisyllabic words in eight quantity types; acoustic (duration, F0, intensity) plus a 30-subject perception test. Harnud stresses that stress is not lexically or morphologically distinctive. Gao 2020 argues the earlier studies confound stress with phrase-edge effects.
new_statements.identity_note: Deciding source (Harnud 2004; also Harnud 2003, Harnud et al. 2000) is an instrumental + perception study of 'Mongolian' as spoken by three natives of Inner Mongolia from Chakhar (Shuluun Höh Banner), two of them Inner Mongolian Radio announcers, i.e. the Chakhar-based Standard Inner Mongolian — the core variety of peri1253 (Chakhar is a dialect of peri1253 in Glottolog; no separate glottocode verified here). The older first-hand statements found (Mostaert 1926 p. 853; Soulié 1903 p. 18) describe the Ordos (Urdus) dialect, also under peri1253 (Georg 2003 'Ordos' is listed among peri1253's Glottolog refs); Gao 2020 describes Khorchin (Eastern Inner Mongolian). Dialects differ: Ordos/Chakhar tradition = initial expiratory accent; Harnud's Chakhar data = quantity-driven (first syllable if long, otherwise second); Khorchin = word-final F0/intensity peak (pitch accent). Not Halh Mongolian (halh1244).

tone_statements.citation: Jin, Zhenglin (金正琳). 2024. チャハルモンゴル語における固有語と外来語のアクセントについて [Chakhar Mongolian word accent for native and loanwords]. 神戸言語学論叢 (Kobe Papers in Linguistics) 14: 1-15. Kobe: 神戸大学人文学研究科言語学研究室. DOI 10.24546/0100487305; hdl 20.500.14094/0100487305.
tone_statements.quote: まず、問題1と問題2について、チャハルモンゴル語にはアクセントがあり、高さアクセントの傾向が強い。次に、問題3について、高さを基準とする場合、固有語のアクセント位置は第2音節に現れるのが一般的である。それに対して、外来語は3音節語のみ第3音節、それ以外は第2音節に現れる結果が判明した。以上の結果は、チャハルモンゴル語は無アクセント言語であるという白音門徳(2014)の主張、そして、第1音節にアクセントが置かれるとする確精扎布(1993)の観点と明確に異なる。また、本稿は、高さでアクセントをより適切に説明できることを根拠とし、高さアクセントの可能性が高いことを論じた。[p.14] ... これらを根拠に、本稿はチャハルモンゴル語に高さに基づくアクセントが存在すると主張する。[p.1]
tone_statements.translation: First, on questions 1 and 2: Chakhar Mongolian has an accent, and it tends strongly to be a pitch accent. Next, on question 3: taking pitch as the criterion, the accent of native words generally appears on the second syllable, whereas for loanwords it turned out to appear on the third syllable only in trisyllabic words and otherwise on the second syllable. These results differ clearly from Bayarmend's (2014) claim that Chakhar Mongolian is an accentless language and from Qujingzhab's (1993) view that the accent is placed on the first syllable. Further, on the grounds that pitch describes the accent more adequately, this paper argued that a pitch accent is the likelier analysis. [p.14] ... On these grounds this paper claims that a pitch-based accent exists in Chakhar Mongolian. [p.1]

tone_statements.citation: Xilingowa (シリンゴワ). 2017. モンゴル語スヌト方言における音声学的アクセントの研究: 実験音声学的アプローチ [Study of phonetic accents in the Mongolian Su'nid dialect: an experimental-phonetic approach]. 実験音声学・言語学研究 (Research in Experimental Phonetics and Linguistics) 9: 155-183. DOI 10.57354/repl.9.0_155.
tone_statements.quote: 筆者の母語であるモンゴル語スヌト方言は、他のモンゴル系諸方言と同様アクセントに音韻論的対立がない。このため、今日までアクセント研究はほとんど行われておらず、定説として「モンゴル語のアクセントは、常に語の第1音節に強さが置かれる」とされてきた。[p.155] ... このようなことが可能なのも、スヌト方言が音韻論的に非示差的である bound accent（拘束アクセント）であるためであろう。[p.173] ... モンゴル語スヌト方言では短母音のみで構成される語を例に取ると、ストレスは第1音節に落ちるがピッチは音節構造に依存して第1だけでなく第2音節以下にも落ちるので〔3〕のタイプといことになる。[p.162] ... 1音節語に用いられている音調パタンは、H、HL の2種類である。[p.179]
tone_statements.translation: The Mongolian Sunid dialect, the author's mother tongue, has, like the other Mongolic dialects, no phonological opposition in accent. For this reason accent has hardly been studied to date, and the received view has been that 'Mongolian accent always places strength on the first syllable of the word'. [p.155] ... That this is possible is presumably because the Sunid dialect has a phonologically non-distinctive bound accent. [p.173] ... In Sunid Mongolian, taking words made up only of short vowels as an example, stress falls on the first syllable but pitch, depending on syllable structure, falls not only on the first but also on the second and later syllables, so it belongs to type [3] (pitch and stress mutually independent). [p.162] ... The pitch patterns used in monosyllabic words are of two kinds, H and HL. [p.179]

sources.note: Production study (Praat; mean dB and semitone re 100 Hz per vowel) of 2-4-syllable native words and 107 loanwords. Concludes that Chakhar Mongolian does have a word accent and that it is best described as a pitch (高さ) accent rather than a stress (強さ) accent: measured by pitch, native words peak regularly on syllable 2 at every word length, loanwords on syllable 3 in trisyllables and otherwise on syllable 2; measured by intensity the peaks scatter. sources.note: A native-speaker experimental study of word 'accent' analysed through pitch. States that Sunid, like the other Mongolian dialects, has no phonological opposition in accent (non-distinctive 'bound accent'); word pitch patterns (per-syllable H, HL, LH, L 音調) are fully predictable from syllable count, syllable weight (long/short) and syllable structure (open/closed): monosyllables H (closed) or HL (open); disyllables start low by default, HL on a long second syllable, LH on a long first syllable, H on a closed second syllable, L on a short first syllable; trisyllables likewise. tone.quote: 筆者の母語であるモンゴル語スヌト方言は、他のモンゴル系諸方言と同様アクセントに音韻論的対立がない。このため、今日までアクセント研究はほとんど行われておらず、定説として「モンゴル語のアクセントは、常に語の第1音節に強さが置かれる」とされてきた。[p.155] ... このようなことが可能なのも、スヌト方言が音韻論的に非示差的である bound accent（拘束アクセント）であるためであろう。[p.173] ... モンゴル語スヌト方言では短母音のみで構成される語を例に取ると、ストレスは第1音節に落ちるがピッチは音節構造に依存して第1だけでなく第2音節以下にも落ちるので〔3〕のタイプといことになる。[p.162] ... 1音節語に用いられている音調パタンは、H、HL の2種類である。[p.179]
tone.locator: p. 155 abstract (要旨), first sentence; p. 173 sec. 3 end ('bound accent'); p. 162 sec. 2.4 end (stress vs pitch independence); pp. 179-180 sec. 5 結論 (pitch-pattern rules).
tone.translation: The Mongolian Sunid dialect, the author's mother tongue, has, like the other Mongolic dialects, no phonological opposition in accent. For this reason accent has hardly been studied to date, and the received view has been that 'Mongolian accent always places strength on the first syllable of the word'. [p.155] ... That this is possible is presumably because the Sunid dialect has a phonologically non-distinctive bound accent. [p.173] ... In Sunid Mongolian, taking words made up only of short vowels as an example, stress falls on the first syllable but pitch, depending on syllable structure, falls not only on the first but also on the second and later syllables, so it belongs to type [3] (pitch and stress mutually independent). [p.162] ... The pitch patterns used in monosyllabic words are of two kinds, H and HL. [p.179]

tone.quote: One, Mongolian words stress has no distinctive function. ... Four, on the whole, the stronger and higher syllable is not fixed on the first syllable in terms of the distribution of the intensity peak or the pitch peak in the polysyllabic words in Mongolian dialects. Finally concluded there is not linguistic sense of the word stress in Mongolian. Although some of the syllable's pronunciation is stronger or higher than else in the polysyllabic words, That is not word stress, just a change of a sound as a result of the pronunciation requirements, or personal pronunciation habits.
